title: Chapter 9 — How to Learn Product: The FAB Framework
intro: Feature, Advantage, Benefit — the system for turning spec sheets into selling knowledge.

sections.title: Specs Do Not Sell — Benefits Do
sections.content:
A spec sheet tells you what a product has. It does not tell you why a customer should care.

The FAB framework converts product knowledge into selling language.

Feature: what the product has. 'This refrigerator has a dual evaporator system.'
Advantage: what it does better. 'That keeps the fridge and freezer environments separate, preventing odour transfer.'
Benefit: why the customer cares. 'Your ice cream will not taste like last night's fish.'

Every feature you learn should be stored in your brain as a complete FAB chain. Feature alone is information. Advantage is interesting. Benefit is what closes the deal.

sections.title: How to Study Product
sections.content:
When you learn a new product, do not try to memorize every spec. Instead, identify the five features that matter most to customers in that category. Build the FAB chain for each one. Practice saying them out loud.

Then go stand in front of the product and demonstrate each one physically. Open the door. Pull the drawer. Show the feature while you say the benefit.

Products are physical. Your knowledge of them should be too.

sections.title: Connecting FAB to Discovery
sections.content:
FAB is only powerful when it connects to what the customer told you during discovery. If you learned they entertain frequently, the flexible shelving benefit is relevant. If they never mentioned entertaining, it is just noise.

The 10 Steps work together. Discovery tells you which FAB chains to use. The demo is where you deliver them. The benefit should always connect back to their life — not just the product.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
When evaluating product knowledge application, ask:

Can the salesperson articulate features as benefits — not just specs?
Do they connect benefits to what they learned during discovery?
Do they demonstrate features physically — or just describe them?
Are they learning new products consistently — or relying on what they already know?
